toc.title: Using your imagination to explore safety

blocks.p: The various Polyvagal primary and mixed states bring different emotions, cognitions, sensations, and impulses. I refer to these as "SSIEC." It's enough to name these domains of your body's experiences for now.

Depending on what Polyvagal State (S) you are in, your Sensation (S), Impulse (I), Emotion (E), and Cognition (C) experiences will change. You already know that "story follows state." Likewise, sensations follow state as do impulses and emotions. (It might be easier to think of "SSIEC" as "S:SIEC," or "S->SIEC," or even "S=SIEC." For visual ease, I'll use "SSIEC" when referring to all the domains and just "SIEC" with one "S" when referring to the sensations, impulses, emotions, and cognitions that stem from the Polyvagal state.)
The SIEC of your safety state is distinct from your other Polyvagal states. I will briefly review each SSIEC domain to help you identify your safety state.

The ventral vagal pathways of your ANS govern your Polyvagal safety state, connected to the nucleus ambiguus of your brainstem. You probably don't directly notice the activation of your ventral vagal pathways. Instead, you will need to rely on the experiential shifts that take place as a result of those pathways activating. When your safety state is active, your sensations, impulses, emotions, and cognitions all shift. You can consciously notice your primary Polyvagal safety state is active due to the distinct safety state flavoring of your other domains (SIEC).

The safety state flavors your cognitions with more connection, optimism, hope, and empathy. From your safety state, you will think more positively and realistically. You may fully be aware of your limitations, but you won't judge yourself for them.

In your safety state, you can look back on a panic attack with compassion for yourself. You'll see how you coped through it and reached the other end. You'll congratulate yourself while also acknowledging there is still room to grow. You won't judge and shame yourself for having a panic attack or for crying in sadness.

Your safety state enables you to empathize with others without getting sucked into their emotional turmoil. You can understand their point of view and connect it to larger shared values. You'll be optimistic for that person, even though you can also acknowledge they have their own struggles.
From safety, you can communicate more effectively, even with difficult topics. You can express your need for healthier boundaries while allowing people to remain in your life as appropriate.
The safety state brings the potential to think critically, learn something new, or question your beliefs without the threat of losing yourself. You have curiosity and interest in yourself and others.

You can exist in stillness from your safety state and notice your surroundings. You will be okay with your mind wandering and seeing where it takes you. You will have more capacity to exist in quiet and even in solitude without your thoughts spiraling into rumination.

The safety state brings awe, wonder, and imagination as well. You may realize your place in the world as something small but instrumental in the larger whole. Or you may experience a deeper connection with your religious and spiritual beliefs. You'll appreciate how others are not inherently better or worse than you but equal in the universe's grand scheme. Safety brings a deep appreciation and humility for your existence.
The safety state is generally affiliated with what we consider to be "positive" emotions:

Safety state emotions come from the Polyvagal primary state of safety, but also include the mixed states involving safety. You may experience the mixed states of intimacy, play, and stillness as you build safety. The mixed states will have unique emotions. For example, relaxation comes from stillness, while spontaneous excitement comes from play.

While the safety state is associated with positive emotions, safety is not always about being happy or feeling good. It's simply about having access to the ventral vagal pathways, which allow you to experience a broader range of positive and negative emotions in a more self-regulated way. These pathways also keep you connected to the present moment, both internally and externally.

One can access the full range of emotions from the safety state, even defensive state emotions. From safety, it's possible to feel the sadness of shutdown, the anxiety of flight, or the anger of fight. But those emotions won't be out of control or dysregulated. You'll eventually allow those emotions while grounded in your safety state, with curiosity and possibly even mindfulness and self-compassion.

Underneath the emotions of safety are the sensations of safety. Your emotions aren't things that exist in your brain. Instead, you can actively notice and feel them in your body. The bodily experiences of emotions are called "sensations."

Let's use calm as an example. Calm is the emotion. The sensations of calm lie underneath the emotion of calm. In other words, when you're calm, how do you know? How can you tell you're calm? What does it feel like to be calm? Where does calm live in your body? What is the felt experience of calmness?

Think back to a time when you actually felt calm. Got it? Now, allow your body to feel that calmness again, as best you can. Take a breath and extend the exhale to help yourself out. After you exhale, look inward and see if you can notice where calmness lives in your body. Do a body scan from your toes to your head. Is there a specific place where calmness lives, or is it more of an entire-body experience? Once you've identified where it lives in your body, then describe what calm feels like. People often describe calm as warm, settled, and connected to self and environment.

The impulses of safety come with the sensations of safety stemming from the Polyvagal safety state. Impulses are actions that your body must do from the state that it's in. For example, when mobilized in flight, running may be an impulse leading to escape.

The safety state has its own impulses, just like the defensive states. Safety impulses involve connection. From safety, there's an impulse to connect with the self and the present moment sensory experience of the environment. There is also an impulse to connect with others, like people and pets. The body will do things like:

ul: smile and use upper facial muscles

blocks.p: The human body possesses natural impulses to maintain balance and promote "health, growth, and restoration." By accessing its homeostatic functions, the body can allocate its resources efficiently. The body uses its resources for survival during dangerous moments. However, the body utilizes its resources to thrive and flourish when the safety state is active.

blocks.h: Using your imagination to explore safety

blocks.p: One of the first things I often do to help clients discover safety is guide them to use their imagination. I'll ask you the same question I ask them: if you could go anywhere right now to feel safe, where would that be? Pretend you have all the money you need and can go wherever you want, real or made-up. You even have a rocket ship if you need to go somewhere far away. Let your imagination create a place for you or think of an actual location you'd go to feel safe. (Another option is to use your memory to recall a past safety experience. But use imagination for now if you can. Memories often bring other emotions with them.)

If you can't imagine a place that feels safe or the wording is too broad, narrow it down. Instead, ask yourself where you would go to feel a specific safety emotion, like calm, relaxed, or content. Or, go even narrower and ask yourself where you would go to breathe easier, smile, or hug someone.
Once you have the place, visualize it more vividly and immerse yourself in its details.

ul: Is there movement in the environment?
What objects do you see? What colors are there?
Is anyone with you? A person? Pet? Or are you alone?
What time of day is it? Where is the sun?
What do you feel on your skin? Can you feel the sun or the air?
Can you taste or touch anything? What do you hear?
What does the ground under your feet feel like? Are you wearing shoes or something else?

blocks.p: Do the best you can to immerse yourself in this imaginary safety place. It's okay if you have a hard time. I find that using imagination is generally an accessible way for people to feel safety, but it's not easy for everyone. If it's a struggle, try using a memory of safety. Think back to a time you last smiled or hugged someone genuinely. And if that's too much, go look your dog or cat in the eyes, smile, and give it some love. Then, notice where you feel safety in your body and what emotions you have. Then use that safety to create a scenario in your imagination to continue to feel it.

Your imaginative place of safety differs from mine, one of my clients, and the next person reading this. Safety is different for each of us on every level: experientially, historically, vagal brake strength, what cues safety, and what anchors us. Be open to what your imagination brings you. There is no wrong answer; take what it gives you and develop it further by answering the imagination prompts listed above.

Mildred imagined standing at the edge of a small lake with a waterfall cascading down into it, creating a misty spray gently caressing her face. Surrounding Mildred were cliffs covered in vibrant greenery, and the sound of crashing water filled the air. She felt completely at peace in this serene and secluded spot, embraced by the environment's soothing sounds and natural beauty.

My place of safety is a small wooden cabin nestled deep within a shady, green forest. The forest ground is a rich brown soil with moss and grass scattered around. The cottage is a minimal and modern wooden structure: simple but warm and inviting. Sunlight streams through a parting of trees and the oversized windows, illuminating the cozy interior filled with plush cushions and soft blankets. No one is allowed here except for my wife and me (apologies to my kids). Two chairs face a large window where we can see the greenery outside. The chairs are close enough for our hands to meet as our arms hang limply.

Clients commonly imagine nature scenes, typically beaches, meadows, and forests. But sometimes they surprise me. One client imagined San Francisco: a busy city full of color and energy. Another imagined a city in France that she wanted to travel to and saw in pictures. And another client imagined living in the sky amongst the clouds. One imagined spending time with a friend at an aquarium with no one else present.

The imaginary safety place you just explored is something you can use as a reliable top-down safety cue. When needed, take a deep breath, extend your exhale and recall your imaginative safety environment. Use this to feel "positive" emotions like calm and content or to ground yourself in the present moment.

The goal now is to take these safety images from your imagination and transform them into actual present moment felt experiences. Basically level up the experience through mindful connection with it. Imagine using your senses in this environment and what experiences they bring.

You need to go beyond just imagining and immerse yourself in the experience mindfully. In other words, what does it feel like to be in that environment? Not just emotionally but in your body. In your non-imaginary body, notice what safety feels like. Here are some basic questions to reflect on as you imagine safety and notice the experiences mindfully in your real body:

ul: Where do you feel safety in your body? Somewhere in particular or all over?
What happens to your breathing as you immerse yourself in the imaginative scene?
Do you feel heavier or lighter?
Are your muscles more tense or more relaxed?

blocks.p: Imagining safety goes beyond just thinking about it. Within your imagination is a full sensory experience to actually feel in your body in the present moment. It's an accessible gateway to safety you can do on your own whenever you need or want it. Am I saying you'll feel perfectly safe, calm and connected when you imagine this? That this solves your problems? Of course not. But it's a place to start.

blocks.why: Imagining safety is an accessible gateway. This practice anchors through your imagination.

blocks.p: As you practice with safety anchors, you may encounter a range of safety-related emotions and sensations. Calmness, peace, serenity, and relaxation might greet you. You could feel a sense of flow, clarity, or newfound motivation. Experiencing a deeper connection, togetherness, and wholeness may also be part of the journey. You might encounter ease, joy, happiness, appreciation, and other emotions that feel generally positive or good. I sincerely hope you do, and I'm sure you do, too.
You may be surprised that you have more reference points for safety than you initially realized. As you engage in the practices, notice how your safety experiences grow in number and variety.

Noticing these potential safety experiences depends on your capacity to feel and embrace safety. The journey is unique for each individual, and it's okay to take it at your own pace, honoring your readiness and comfort levels.

blocks.prompt: Where is your imaginary safety place?
What thoughts would you have in this place?
Are you noticing any sensations? What are they?
Do you notice an impulse to connect with anyone or anything within the imaginary safety space?
